content_html:
Shared Neural Architecture

Perception vs Conceptual Thought

The brain reuses the same hierarchical circuits for perception and for imagination and conceptual reasoning. The difference is not a separate module, but a shift in direction and precision-weighting of signals in a predictive loop: bottom-up sensory evidence vs top-down generative predictions, gated by control systems.

Both modes use the same circuits. What changes is which direction dominates and how strongly prediction errors are weighted (precision).

How the brain tells the difference

Precision weighting: sensory prediction errors are amplified in perception; dampened during imagery/thought (gating in ACC/parietal/cerebellum).
Motor & sensory gating: in REM or focused imagery, external input/output are partly inhibited while the model runs internally.
Source monitoring: hippocampus–prefrontal systems tag representations with context and confidence (real vs imagined).
Executive control: prefrontal cortex constrains free-running imagery to task goals, keeping concepts coherent.

Continuum of modes

Mode Signal balance Phenomenology Example
Perception Bottom-up >> Top-down Vivid, externally anchored Seeing a street
Imagery / Memory Balanced Less vivid, recall-bound Remembering yesterday
Conceptual reasoning Top-down > Bottom-up Abstract, schema-driven Working through a proof
Dreaming (REM) Top-down >> Bottom-up Vivid but unbound by input Unconstrained narrative

Practice: deliberate switching

Grounding pulse: glance at 3 real anchors (visual, auditory, interoceptive) to increase bottom-up precision.
Imagination pulse: close eyes, reduce external input, walk a spatial schema to increase top-down drive.
Reality check: ask “What prediction would be falsified by immediate input?” to retag imagined content.
